passages.title: The searching lamp overturns confidence in indifference
passages.summary: The LORD’s word comes to Zephaniah in the days of King Josiah. God will sweep everything from the face of the earth. He will strike Judah and those who worship Baal and the stars. Some swear by the LORD and also by another god. The day of the LORD is near. He will search Jerusalem with lamps. He will punish those who say he does nothing, good or bad. It will be a day of wrath, and silver and gold will not save.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected places named in the warning and promise. No attack or return path is reconstructed.

lds.text: The lesson asks readers to examine attitudes and conduct condemned in the opening warning. What assumption does God’s searching lamp expose?

contextNote.title: The searching lamp overturns confidence in indifference
contextNote.text: Verse 12 does not describe open rebels. It describes people “settled on their dregs,” like wine left too long. They are comfortable and undisturbed. Their belief is that the LORD will do nothing either way. They treat God as beside the point. The lamps mean that no corner of the city stays dark. Verse 13 takes the wealth and houses they rely on.

passages.title: An uncertain refuge stands beside the ruin of proud cities
passages.summary: Zephaniah calls the nation to gather before the day of anger comes. The humble of the land should seek the LORD. They should seek righteousness and humility. Perhaps they will be sheltered on that day. Philistia’s cities will be emptied. Moab and Ammon will become like Sodom for their pride. Ethiopia will fall by the sword. Nineveh, which said no one was like it, will become a home for wild animals.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected places named in the warning and promise. No attack or return path is reconstructed.

lds.text: The lesson contrasts pride with seeking humility before God. Why does possible shelter remain uncertain even for those who seek humility?

contextNote.title: An uncertain refuge stands beside the ruin of proud cities
contextNote.text: Verse 3 speaks to people who are already humble and obedient. They are told to keep seeking. The verse then says “It may be.” Shelter is hoped for and not promised as payment. Around this verse, nations fall on every side. Philistia lies west, Moab and Ammon east, Ethiopia south, and Assyria north. Nineveh’s boast in verse 15 is the kind only God may make.

passages.title: The gathered people differ from the leaders who consumed them
passages.summary: Zephaniah cries woe to the rebellious city that listens to no one. Its officials are roaring lions, and its judges are wolves. Its prophets are reckless, and its priests profane what is holy. The LORD within it does no wrong and gives justice every morning. He will purify the speech of the nations to call on his name. He will leave a humble and lowly people in the city. Zion is told to sing, for the LORD is among them. He will save the lame and gather the outcasts.

lds.text: The lesson connects the promised joy with a later scene in 3 Nephi 17. How do the gathered people differ from the earlier city’s rulers?

contextNote.title: The gathered people differ from the leaders who consumed them
contextNote.text: Verses 3–4 describe rulers who devour like lions and wolves. Verse 12 describes the people who remain: humble and lowly. Verse 13 says they do no wrong and tell no lies. Verse 19 names those God gathers: the lame and the driven out. These are the kind of people the old rulers consumed. Their shame is turned to praise. Verse 17 pictures God himself singing over them.
